title: A contact path for an independent school
metaTitle: Contact path for an independent school
excerpt: Say who reads an inquiry, how soon they reply, and what a parent should have ready. A visit stays the main action. A ten-field form loses families.
alt: A long, quiet office corridor with glass rooms, a teal sofa, and a dark kitchen, a place where a named person might actually read the mail.
caption: The corridor is empty until you know who sits in it. The inquiry page should name that person. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the contact page for?
faqs.answer: Questions a published visit date cannot hold: support you should discuss first, a move from another city, or a year that is already full. Open mornings should be bookable without this form. Say that at the top so families do not write to ask the time.

faqs.question: Which fields are enough?
faqs.answer: The child's year, a parent's name, an email, and the question. Add a way to say visit or question if the page does both. Leave off employers, how they heard of you, and an essay about the child. Ask for sensitive documents only when you are ready to hold a specific one.

faqs.question: What should happen after send?
faqs.answer: The screen and the email should name the role that replies and the window you actually keep, including holidays if you are slow then. Say that the message does not hold a place. Labels on the form should stay visible, and errors should name the missing field.

markdown:
An independent school contact page should tell a parent deciding where a child will spend years what happens after they reach out, how soon a person replies, and what to have ready. The action is to visit or inquire. A form with ten fields is a way to lose a family that had one question and a phone in the pickup line.

WCAG's understandable principle is the right standard for this page. The form should explain itself. Labels stay visible. Errors say what to fix. The result tells the parent what will happen next. A form that only the office understands is a locked gate with a nicer typeface.

## Visit first, messages second

Most families do not need a correspondence to begin. They need a date when they can walk the day, or a short inquiry if a visit is not possible yet. The contact page should say that at the top, with the visit link in the same words as the header. Treat the form as the path for what a date cannot hold.

Say which questions belong here. A child who needs support you should discuss before a tour. A move into the area next year. A year group that the dates page already marks as full, if you still welcome a conversation about the following year. A correction to a visit that is already booked. If you list these, families self-sort. If you do not, they will use the form to ask what time the open morning is, and you will answer by hand until you resent the website.

Do not make "Inquire" the only verb if "Visit" is the real next step for local families in the admissions window. One path for the visit. A clearly secondary form for the exception.

If a year is closed, say so above the form. Do not invite a long letter that you will answer with a no you could have printed. Closed years deserve a sentence and, if true, the next year you expect to open. Hope should not be a form field.

## What happens after they send it

The confirmation on the screen has to be specific. "Submitted" is not enough. Say who receives it, in a role a parent can picture: the registrar, or the head of the junior school, not "the admissions team" if that team is one person on Tuesdays. Say whether the reply comes by email. Say whether you phone. If you do not phone, say that, so a parent is not waiting for a call you never place.

If the office does not read mail over the weekend, say so beside the form and again in the confirmation. A message sent on Sunday night should not sound as if a person is already reviewing the child's future. Promise the window you keep. "By the end of the next school day" is a real promise if it is true. A faster promise you miss is worse than a slower one you keep. Families are comparing you with two other offices. The reliable one feels safer.

Say what this message does not do. It does not hold a place. It does not start an assessment you do not run. It does not skip a visit that you still require. Limits in the confirmation prevent a hopeful reading of a vague thank-you. The name and the window are what make the note human.

Copy the same sentences into the email receipt. The parent will lose the page and keep the email.

## How fast, said so you can keep it

Speed is a fact about the office rota, not a brand attribute. Look at the last twenty inquiries and write the window that would have been true for all of them, not the window from your best week in September. Publish that. Then staff it. A page that says "we reply within the hour" while the only reader is teaching until three is a fiction.

If the window differs in the holidays, say so. Independent schools often go quiet in August and hide it because a 24-hour admissions desk sounds more serious. You are not that desk. "During term, by the next school day. In the summer holiday, once a week" is a shape a family can plan around. Silence plus a slow reply feels like indifference, even when everyone is simply away.

Name the backup. When the registrar is out, who reads the form, and does the window change? If the answer is nobody, change the page before the leave, not after the thread. The about page's names should match this duty. If Mr Shah reads inquiries, Mr Shah can be mentioned here without a biography.

Do not display a live chat you do not attend. A sleeping chat is a form with worse expectations. If someone can truly answer during published hours, say the hours and close the widget outside them. An always-on badge that nobody attends makes the school look careless.

## What to have ready

Tell them what makes a useful reply possible. The child's year, or the year they would enter. The question in a few sentences. An email you can answer. A phone number only if you might need to call, not as a toll on a simple note. For a support question: the kind of need, in the family's words, and whether they want that conversation before a visit. For a relocation: the month you would arrive. For a booked visit that needs a change: the date you already hold.

That is the core. The other parent's job title, the child's hobbies, a personal statement, and a postal address are not required to answer most pre-visit questions. Ask for them later, inside a process the family has chosen, if you truly use them. Required fields should be the ones this reply needs.

Tell them not to attach sensitive documents until you have asked for a specific one. Medical reports and reports from a previous school do not belong in a first web form "just in case." Say where those documents should go, and when. A box that invites every file will receive files you are not ready to hold carefully.

If a question is only "what time is the open morning," point at the list and do not make them write. Every answer you can publish deletes a message. The form gets better as the rest of the site gets more specific. Fees, the end of the day, the stair, the closed year: none of those should require a correspondence.

## The ten-field form

Count the fields. Child's year, parent name, email, and the question will cover almost every legitimate first message. A fifth field for "visit or a question" is reasonable if the page handles both. A form becomes hostile as it nears ten: both parents' occupations, how you heard about the school, a religion dropdown, a marketing opt-in already switched on, country, postal address, child's current school, a second phone, a captcha that fails on the pavement, a required essay titled "tell us about your child."

Each extra field is a reason to return to the school that published its open morning and its fee. The comparison is open on the phone while they decide whether your form respects them.

"How did you hear about us" is your marketing question. Ask it at a visit, if you must, of people who came. Do not charge the first inquiry with it. An essay about the child before anyone has said hello asks a family to perform intimacy on cue. You will learn more in twenty minutes in the corridor. Save the form for logistics and for the questions that need privacy.

Use labels that remain visible, not placeholders that vanish as typing starts. A parent should be able to check what they entered. WCAG's understandable principle shows up in that small requirement. Errors should name the field. "Please complete all required fields" is not an error. "Add an email so the registrar can reply" is.

The button should say "Send the question" or "Request a visit," not "Submit." After it is pressed, do not invite a double send. Show the confirmation where the form was, especially on a phone, so nobody hunts for a banner above a crest.

## Questions a date cannot answer

Write three short examples near the form. "We move to the city in April. Is a visit useful before we have an address?" "Our child needs support with reading. Who should we speak to before we book?" "Year 5 looks full. Are you speaking with families about the following year?" Examples teach scope and length. Parents will mimic the length you show. Two lines are a gift to the person who must answer.

Answer the stable three on the page, above the form. The end time of the day. Whether you have a bus. Whether a year is open. Publishing them is how the contact page stays a side door instead of becoming the whole school, badly retold in an inbox.

For questions you should not answer in public, the form is right. A specific child's needs. A complaint. A family situation. Say that a named role reads these, and repeat the window.

Link to the day and the fees when the worry is one you have already described. "If you are asking about the yard, the junior page shows the rota." You may point at your own limits. It reduces mail and respects a parent willing to read.

## Where the path sits

Link this path from the footer and from any page that creates exceptions: support, a full year, a visit that needs a human. Do not make it the main button on the homepage if the main action is an open morning a parent can book. A site with two equal buttons, "Visit" and "Contact," will receive visit requests as unstructured mail. Then the office will blame families for being unclear. The families followed the weight you designed.

The heading should say this is a question or a visit request. "Ask the office" is clear. "Get in touch" is fog. Prefer the clearer heading. Parents skim, and the heading is the skim.

Put the gate, the hour, and a phone number for the morning of a visit on this page even if they live elsewhere. People open "contact" to find the door. A form without a door generates messages that only ask where you are. Publish the door. Then the form can be about the child.

When the path is this tight, the remaining risk is the rest of the site: the mission line, the crest film, the pages that perform a school you do not run. [What to take off the site so the day and the visit can do their work](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-an-independent-school) is the next piece. It is the edit that keeps this form from becoming a dumping ground.

If you want that path tested against a real week of inquiries, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the form and five real questions, with the names removed. The fields you never used are the ones to cut.
